subtype: Drawing and early writing of messages [Expressing]
passage: Note from Jomon, nursery teacher. Avni (5) gave me a card: a big yellow circle, a row of wavy lines she called "writing", and a stick figure with a huge smile. She read it aloud. "Dear Miss, thank you for the story, love Avni." I didn't correct the letters. I said, "Thank you, I love the smile." She grinned and asked me to hang it up, so it went beside the window. 🙂

qa.q: What did Avni call the wavy lines?
qa.a: Writing.

qa.q: What was Avni feeling when she gave Jomon the card?
qa.a: Affection and gratitude, shown by the smiling figure and the words she read out. She may also have wanted to please him.

qa.q: How should an adult respond to a card like this?
qa.a: To the meaning and the picture, not the spelling.

qa.q: How might Jomon feel receiving Avni's card?
qa.a: Jomon seems touched and pleased, giving thanks, praising the smile and hanging the card by the window.

grounding: Shows a preschooler drawing and scribbling a thank-you card, with an adult responding to the meaning rather than the spelling.

subtype: Drawing and early writing of messages [Expressing]
passage: On the courtyard step of the village house, Keerthana, six, scribbled wavy lines, a boat and a big red heart on the back of a calendar page. "It says, Papa, come home soon," she told her grandmother. They held it up to the phone camera. Her father Sahil, working in another town, leaned close to the screen. "I can read it. Come home soon. Thank you, beta. I'm counting the days."

qa.q: What did Keerthana say her message said?
qa.a: "Papa, come home soon."

qa.q: What might Keerthana feel about her father being away?
qa.a: She probably misses him, shown by the message and the big heart. She may also be excited to show him her work.

qa.q: How did Sahil respond to the drawing?
qa.a: He responded to the meaning, reading it out and thanking her, and did not comment on the spelling.

qa.q: How might Sahil feel seeing the message on the screen?
qa.a: Touched, and perhaps a little homesick.

grounding: Shows a preschooler drawing and scribbling a message of longing to a parent, met with warmth for the meaning.

subtype: Drawing and early writing of messages [Expressing]
passage: On Mother's Day in Melbourne, Tuan gave his mum, Rania, a folded card. Inside was a big red heart, two stick people holding hands, and a line of wiggly marks. “What does it say?” Rania asked. Tuan pointed along the squiggles. “It says, ‘Mummy, you are the best and I love you and you make good noodles.’” Rania didn't mention that none of the marks were letters. She hugged him. “That's the best card I've ever had.” She stood it on the kitchen shelf.

qa.q: Where did Rania stand the card?
qa.a: On the kitchen shelf.

qa.q: What was Tuan feeling as he pointed along the squiggles?
qa.a: He felt proud and loving, sure his marks carried his message to his mum.

qa.q: Why was Rania's response wise?
qa.a: She responded to his meaning and love instead of correcting the spelling, which encourages him to keep sharing feelings in writing.

qa.q: What would change if Rania had said the squiggles weren't real words?
qa.a: Tuan might feel his message didn't count and be less eager to write or draw for people again.

grounding: A preschooler draws and scribbles a card for his mother, and she responds to the meaning rather than the spelling.

subtype: Drawing and early writing of messages [Expressing]
passage: Rafiq's best friend had been off sick from KG for a week. Rafiq drew a picture of the two of them on the swings and wrote underneath: “GT WEL SUN RFQ.” He took it to Seema Ma'am. “Can you send it?” Seema read it aloud: “Get well soon, from Rafiq.” She didn't circle any letters. “Your friend will love this. The swings look fun.” She put it in an envelope, and Rafiq wrote a wobbly R on the back.

qa.q: What did Rafiq write under his picture?
qa.a: “GT WEL SUN RFQ.”

qa.q: What was Rafiq feeling when he drew the card?
qa.a: He was missing his friend and feeling caring, wanting him to get better and come back to the swings.

qa.q: Why was it wise for Seema Ma'am not to circle any letters?
qa.a: It kept the focus on Rafiq's kind message rather than his spelling, so he feels his writing works.

qa.q: How might Rafiq's friend feel receiving the card?
qa.a: He would likely feel happy and missed, seeing his friend's drawing of them on the swings.

grounding: A preschooler writes a get-well card in early spelling, and his teacher responds to the meaning rather than the spelling.

subtype: Drawing and early writing of messages [Expressing]
passage: I'm Omkar, Pema's big brother. For Papa's birthday, Pema made a card with crayons: a yellow sun, Papa with a very long moustache, and lots of zigzags. She held it up and “read” it: “Happy birthday Papa, you are big and strong and funny.” Papa laughed at the moustache and hugged her. He didn't ask what the zigzags said; he just said, “I'll keep this forever.” I don't know if she knew her writing wasn't real letters yet, but she looked so proud.

qa.q: What did Pema draw on Papa?
qa.a: A very long moustache.

qa.q: What was Pema feeling as she read her card aloud?
qa.a: She felt proud and loving, confident her zigzags carried her message to Papa.

qa.q: What did Papa do that encouraged Pema?
qa.a: He laughed warmly, hugged her and treasured the card without asking what the zigzags said.

qa.q: How does Omkar see Pema's writing?
qa.a: Omkar isn't sure she knows her marks aren't real letters yet, but notices how proud she is.

grounding: A brother observes a preschooler read her scribbled birthday card aloud, and their father responds to the meaning.

subtype: Drawing and early writing of messages [Expressing]
passage:
Monday: Pallavi drew a big flower and covered the page in squiggly "letters." "It's for Amma!" Her aunt looked and said, "Those aren't real letters." Pallavi scrunched the card behind her back.

The next Sunday: another card appeared on Keerthana's pillow, full of squiggles and a purple heart. Keerthana sat on the bed. "Will you read it to me?"

Pallavi pointed. "It says I love you. And sorry I spilled the paint."

Keerthana hugged her. "Thank you. That's a beautiful message."

By the end of the month, little squiggle notes were tucked everywhere.

qa.q: What did Pallavi draw on the card on the next Sunday?
qa.a: Squiggles and a purple heart.

qa.q: What was Pallavi feeling when she scrunched the card behind her back on Monday?
qa.a: She was most likely hurt and embarrassed after her aunt said the letters weren't real. It seemed to make her feel her message didn't count.

qa.q: What did Keerthana do that helped Pallavi share her feelings?
qa.a: She asked Pallavi to read the card and responded to the message, love and sorry, rather than the spelling.

qa.q: How does Keerthana's response change things for Pallavi over the month?
qa.a: Pallavi feels her notes are welcomed, so she keeps writing and tucks little squiggle notes everywhere.

grounding: It shows a preschooler writing a scribbled card to share love and an apology, and an adult responding to the meaning rather than the spelling.
